newsitem.title: JAPAN: Four-power Korea peace treaty is no cure-all.
newsitem.headline: Four-power Korea peace treaty is no cure-all.

text.p: Any peace treaty signed by the two Koreas, China and the United States formally ending the 1950-1953 Korean War would not automatically resolve larger security issues plaguing the region.

Rather, concluding a peace treaty could spark a diplomatic tug-of-war between China and the United States over which power maintains bigger influence over the two Koreas, the top North Korea analyst at Japan's defence ministry said on Monday.
At stake in such a possible future Sino-U.S. rivalry would be Korean reunification, one of the biggest unresolved issues in East Asia from World War Two.
The reunification question is also linked to the possibility of setting up a lasting security framework in Asia, similiar to that which has operated in Europe since World War Two.
North and South Korea remain technically at war. The 1950-53 conflict, in which China sided with the North and the United States with the South, ended with an armistice, not a treaty.

Since Stalinist North Korea last week attended preliminary discussions on four-party peace talks, analysts for the first time in decades are daring to speculate about what decreased tension on the Korean peninsula could mean for the region.
"The most predictable state of affairs after signing such a peace treaty would be confusion," Defence Ministry analyst Hideshi Takesada told Reuters in an interview.
"A key point will be whether the United States can persuade North Korea into entering a full-fledged dialogue with South Korea after the treaty."
If the peace treaty were signed without promises of a North-South dialogue, anti-U.S. sentiment in South Korea would grow, Takesada said.
If that happened, Seoul might pull out from commitments like food aid and funds for nuclear power plants in North Korea -- and it would be back to stalemate.

Another military analyst, Haruo Fujii, said a peace treaty may put an end to North Korea's "rogue" behaviour, such as last year's intrusion of a North submarine into South Korea, and pave the way for a larger security framework.
But both analysts predicted that U.S. troops would stay in South Korea even after a peace treaty.
"They would be something like the token U.S. military presence in Germany under the NATO umbrella," Fujii said.
Any peace treaty would probably mean that the United States established diplomatic ties with North Korea, a subject anathema to South Korea and a major embarrassment for Japan.
Japan would be left as the only regional player without diplomatic ties with North Korea.
If a peace treaty were signed, the next challenge for China and the United States would be how to cope with a reunification of the Koreas.
"After a peace treaty, the first signs of an eventual reunification may be signs of pan-Korean nationalism replacing their rival ideologies," Takesada said.
"In the long run, both China and the United States would try their best to maintain influence in a would-be reunified Korea."
But Takesada, Fujii and other Japanese analysts said the conclusion of a peace treaty could take years, if if happened at all.
"There are too many variables, such as whether North Korea will accept South Korea as a full-fledged party in the main talks," Takesada said.
